CausalChain: HepG2 cells exhibit low CYP450 expression and metabolic activity -> This deficiency correlates with epigenetic marks (e.g., DNA hypermethylation, histone deacetylation) that silence key drug-metabolizing genes -> Targeted epigenetic modulators can reverse these modifications -> Reactivation of CYP450 and related enzymes enhances metabolic capacity -> Improved metabolic function makes the cells a more faithful model of normal hepatocytes
Hypothesis: Reversing epigenetic repression in HepG2 cells through targeted treatment will restore the expression and activity of drug‐metabolizing enzymes, thereby converting this hepatoblastoma-like cell line into a more physiologically relevant model for studying hepatocyte drug metabolism and toxicity.
Abstract: We hypothesize that the low expression of key drug‐metabolizing enzymes observed in HepG2 cells is not an intrinsic permanent feature of the cell line but is largely due to reversible epigenetic suppression. By treating HepG2 cells with targeted epigenetic modulators, such as DNA demethylating agents or histone deacetylase inhibitors, it may be possible to reactivate the expression of cytochrome P450 isoforms and other phase I enzymes. Such reactivation would, in turn, render the HepG2 cell line more comparable to primary hepatocytes and enhance its utility in drug metabolism and toxicity testing, especially in the context of hepatoblastoma modeling.
